Historical Perspective

The Digital Age: A Social History

Technology does not emerge from a vacuum. These milestones show how social forces and technical change co-produce each other.

1969

ARPANET Goes Live

Funded by the US Defense Department, ARPANET laid the packet-switching foundations of the internet—a Cold War military project that transformed global communication.

1984

The Personal Computer & Cultural Shift

Apple's "1984" ad cast computing as liberation from conformity. The PC moved technology from institutions to individuals—but access remained sharply stratified by class.

1991

The World Wide Web Opens

Tim Berners-Lee released the WWW publicly, refusing to patent it. That ethical choice shaped an open, decentralized architecture that changed everything.

1998–2004

The Platform Economy Emerges

Google, Wikipedia, and Facebook launched within six years. "Free" services traded privacy for access, inaugurating surveillance capitalism as the dominant digital business model.

2007

The Smartphone Reconfigures Society

The iPhone restructured attention, labor, intimacy, and public space. Gig economy platforms soon exploited always-on connectivity to create a new precarious workforce.

2016–2018

Algorithmic Reckoning

Cambridge Analytica, Facebook's role in Myanmar's genocide, and deepfakes forced a global reckoning with how platforms algorithmically amplify harm at scale.

2022–present

The Generative AI Inflection

Large language models enter public life. Authorship, labor displacement, epistemic trust, and AI safety now dominate policy agendas worldwide—a live STS experiment.
